articles.title_orig: Election Updates: Trump Heads to Montana After Rally in Arizona; Talarico Keeps His Edge in Tightening Texas Senate Race
articles.title_zh: Election Updates: Trump Heads to Montana After Rally in Arizona; Talarico Keeps His Edge in Tightening Texas Senate Race
articles.content_orig:

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
President Donald Trump has rated tech billionaire Elon Musk ’s intelligence, saying that his frenemy has “a little problem.”
Trump hosted a rally in Bullhead City, Arizona , Wednesday to campaign for Congressman Andy Biggs, who is running against Democratic incumbent Katie Hobbs for governor in the Grand Canyon State.
The president bashed Hobbs, calling her “horrible” and a “dumb person.” He then contrasted Hobbs’ intelligence with that of Musk, who founded the electric car company Tesla , rocket manufacturer SpaceX and artificial intelligence startup xAI.
“I know smart people. I deal from Elon [Musk] down to Katie [Hobbs],” Trump said.
But then the president threw in a slight jab: “Elon’s 80 percent super genius — and 20 percent he got a little problem, I always tell him. He’s a great guy, though.”
Trump and Musk have had a tumultuous relationship. Musk stumped for Trump in the 2024 election and financially backed his campaign.
When Trump returned to the White House for a second term, he brought Musk with him. The tech tycoon led the newly created Department of Government Efficiency, or DOGE, for a couple of months, gutting federal agencies in the name of reducing government waste.
In May 2025, Musk left the White House after he publicly criticized Trump’s massive “big, beautiful” spending bill.
Since the start of July, Musk has donated more than $276 million to help Republican candidates in November’s midterm elections, The New York Times first revealed Monday.
About $158 million of Musk’s money went to the Senate Leadership Fund, the main super PAC backing GOP Senate candidates in the midterms, according to figures provided by the billionaire’s team.
Arizona is the latest stop on Trump’s campaign tour as he hopes to boost Republicans' chances in the midterms.
While the party in power typically loses seats in the midterms, GOP candidates are even struggling in red states like Texas and Ohio.
Trump has called on his supporters to go to the polls and “pretend that I’m on the ballot,” all while facing his own record-low approval ratings.
A whopping 65 percent of Americans disapproved of Trump’s job as president, while just 32 percent approved in a recent Reuters /Ipsos poll. The administration has been dogged by an unpopular war in Iran , a high cost of living and an immigration crackdown that critics have called too aggressive.
Trump was in Bullead City Wednesday to stump for Biggs and congressional candidates Mark Lamb and Abe Hamadeh.
“We gotta elect this guy,” Trump said of Biggs Wednesday. “I'm here to help him and some of your great congressmen.”
Hobbs had a nearly 17-point lead over Biggs, 50.5 to 33.7 percent, in a newly released poll from HighGround Public Affairs consultants.
At Wednesday’s rally, Trump also boasted about his Qatari-gifted Boeing 747 jet worth about $400 million that he has been criticized for accepting.
“When you’re given gifts, you take them, right?” Trump told the crowd about the new Air Force One that he flew in on. “When they give you a 747, you say two words — thank you.”

articles.title_orig: Iranian attacks sink two ships in Strait of Hormuz
articles.title_zh: Iranian attacks sink two ships in Strait of Hormuz
articles.content_orig:
Vessels were hit by missiles as rise in strikes suggests Iran is trying to close waterway before US midterm elections
Two container ships near the strait of Hormuz have ⁠sunk after being struck by missiles, amid the sharpest rise in Iranian attacks on shipping since the start of the US-Israel war with Iran .
The increase in attacks suggests Iran is trying to fully close the strategic waterway in an attempt to frustrate Donald Trump’s efforts to bring down fuel prices before the US midterm elections on 3 November.
The Trump administration has been attempting to deflect attention from the economic impact of the war on Iran by blaming Ukraine’s attacks on Russian refineries for increased fuel prices.
On Wednesday, UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) reported at least five incidents including drone strikes in the previous 48 hours targeting tankers and other commercial ships around the Hormuz area.
“There is a tempo increase in strikes, which looks deliberate,” one maritime security source said.
The Singapore-flagged ​container ‌ship GFS Pride sank on Wednesday after an attack the previous day. Hours later, the Antigua- and Barbuda-flagged Cape Dao sank close to the strait, having been hit by a ​projectile ​on 23 September, according to data from ‌the ‌International Maritime Organization.
Apparently referring to the GFS Pride, Iran said a cargo ship had sunk after hitting a naval mine while making an unauthorised passage through the strait.
State television quoted a statement from Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) that said the ship was travelling on an “illegal and dangerous route” when it hit the mine.
The ship, which was shown tilted in the water and spewing a thick plume of smoke, was carrying 2,500 containers, the broadcast said.
However, UKMTO suggested that both ships had been hit by unidentified projectiles, raising questions over Tehran’s account.
Iran has repeatedly warned ships against trying to transit through the strait without its approval. The US military has been guiding ships through the waterway on a route nearer to Oman’s coast.
Ships in the area were reporting an intense series of attacks in recent days, with six vessels attacked on Sunday alone, according to UKMTO’s monitoring.
Analysis by the Financial Times said 24 ships were hit in the two weeks to 11 October. Of the vessels hit, three were refined energy product tankers and two others were crude oil tankers.
The increased tempo of Iranian attacks appears to have caused a dramatic drop-off in oil shipments through the strait, as Tehran appears determined to demonstrate its ability to strike ships before the US midterms that will decide control of Congress.
US fuel prices have surged by almost 70% since Trump launched his war on Iran, and the Republican party is bracing for punishment at the polls.
According to two Iranian officials, Iran has recently begun using new tactics against vessels it considers to be in violation of its restrictions. The strategy included a change in the type as well as the pace of attacks, with one goal being ⁠to influence the outcome of the US vote, they said.
“The aim is to frustrate efforts by the United States and its allies to bring down global oil prices,” one of the two officials told Reuters.
The decision to adopt the new ​strategy had been taken at the highest levels of Iran’s leadership and was fully coordinated across the country’s ‌ruling system, the officials added.
A US military official, ‌speaking on condition of anonymity, confirmed that Tehran had changed tactics in one significant way. After the US destroyed much of Iran’s radar capabilities, the IRGC had started using unarmed spotters in small boats to ‌identify potential targets, including American naval vessels, the official said.
Last week, in a previously unreported incident, the US military determined that Iranian spotters were operating from a dhow, calling in targets to the IRGC, the official said. US forces confronted the vessel, told its occupants to abandon ship and then destroyed it. There were no casualties, the US official said.

articles.title_orig: How China Profits from the Iran War Without Joining It
articles.title_zh: How China Profits from the Iran War Without Joining It
articles.content_orig:
Diplomacy is often strategic theater, and the performance in Beijing on September 16 was difficult to miss. That day, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi welcomed Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi into the Chinese capital, just days before President Trump’s White House summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping. The timing made Beijing's decision to receive Iran's top diplomat particularly conspicuous. Wang’s description of China and Iran as "comprehensive strategic partners" therefore carried far more weight than a routine handshake. By publicly emphasizing the partnership at this moment, Wang turned an ordinary diplomatic meeting into a signal Washington could not ignore.
Wang urged "all parties" to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, a chokepoint that carried about a fifth of the world's oil and gas before the war, yet stopped short of pressing Iran directly and offered no mediation plan. Beijing reminded Washington that its influence over Iran still matters to the ongoing Iran-U.S. conflict, without committing to leverage that influence in the manner that Washington sought.
Much of China’s influence in Iran stems from its role as an economic lifeline, specifically through two channels: money and matériel. China is Iran's largest trading partner and the primary buyer of its crude oil, most of which is refined by independent "teapot" refineries kept largely outside the international financial system. In a September 2026 op-ed for The Bureau , geopolitical analyst Guermantes Lailari estimated that China buys roughly 90 percent of Iran's crude oil exports, providing Tehran with about $31.2 billion in annual revenue.
Although that figure represents only one assessment, the direction is indisputable, and Washington has attempted to squeeze the arrangement. The U.S. Treasury Department sanctioned a teapot refinery in April and warned two Chinese banks of secondary sanctions if Iranian funds moved through their accounts. However, sanctions experts have long argued that independent Chinese refiners are relatively insulated from U.S. sanctions because of their limited exposure to the U.S. financial system. This blunts the impact of Trump’s threats and renders China’s teapot loophole exceptionally resilient. This arrangement distributes the costs of sanctions onto smaller commercial actors, allowing Beijing to preserve access to Iranian oil while minimizing its own vulnerability to direct economic coercion.
China’s second source of leverage stems from its support for Iranian military capacity, a relationship far harder to see than the oil trade. While oil moves in tankers that can be tracked via satellite, military-related supplies move more discreetly. Dual-use chemicals and components are shipped by shell companies and routed through third-country ports under the guise of ordinary commerce. Those supplies then move through the chains that sustain Iran’s weapons manufacturing.
Iran Watch has traced repeated shipments of missile-propellant ingredients from China to Iran during the 2026 war with the United States and Israel, including through a procurement network that has moved hundreds of metric tons of precursor chemicals since 2023. Chinese industrial inputs have thus become deeply integrated into the infrastructure enabling Iran to replenish its military capabilities under pressure.
The U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission notes that China facilitates Iran's access to export-controlled dual-use technology through transshipment networks and shell companies in Hong Kong, mainland China, and third countries, including critical components used in Iranian drone and missile programs. Iran's arsenal, in other words, depends not only on what it can produce domestically, but on foreign suppliers. China can therefore shape Iran's ability to sustain its military capabilities without entering the conflict directly simply by choosing whether to keep critical supply lines open.
Beijing has stockpiled oil, but its reserves are finite, and a prolonged closure of the Strait of Hormuz would eventually starve the economy that Chinese power rests on. China therefore seeks to reopen the strait on terms it helps dictate, explaining why it maintains close ties to Tehran without pressuring it.
The Washington summit showed as much. Trump and Xi agreed that Iran should not develop nuclear weapons and that in ternational waterways should remain free of transit tolls, but the summit produced no publicly announced Chinese commitment to use economic pressure or diplomatic leverage to compel Tehran to negotiate . Beijing has a clear interest in restoring shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, yet its public position has emphasized restraint rather than coercive measures against Tehran.
China need not declare a side to profit from both outcomes. Its influence runs through oil revenue routed via sanctions-resistant refineries and a quieter flow of dual-use materials that never appear as arms sales. Because both move as ordinary commerce, they give Beijing leverage over the conflict without the costs of openly taking a side. As Trump heads toward APEC in Shenzhen and the G20 in Miami, Washington will have another opportunity to ask China to use its leverage over Iran. The difficulty is that this support is disguised as trade, leaving Washington little to pressure Beijing directly.

articles.title_orig: New White House press secretary Katie Zacharia faces mounting questions about resume
articles.title_zh: New White House press secretary Katie Zacharia faces mounting questions about resume
articles.content_orig:
The new White House press secretary is facing mounting questions about her background and resume as she transitions into her role as the public face of the Trump administration.
Katie Zacharia has long described herself as a lawyer as she has worked to establish herself as a commentator for conservative outlets like Fox News and Newsmax. But so far, she and the White House have offered no evidence that she passed the bar exam in any state or in China, where she worked for a large law firm years ago.
The questions add to the confusion surrounding U.S. President Donald Trump's decision to hire Zacharia, who had worked for his social media company for only a few months when he announced her appointment and whose debut at the podium on Tuesday has been widely panned .
Afterward, the president was asked by reporters where Zacharia had passed the bar exam, following a report by the independent outlet Popular Information that she did not appear to be licensed in any state.
Trump stepped aside to allow Zacharia to answer.
"When I moved to China," she responded over the sound of Marine One whirring in the background. It is not clear what she had intended to say or whether she had finished the sentence.
New White House press secretary stumbles in first briefing | Hanomansing Live
China's notoriously difficult National Unified Legal Professional Qualification Examination can only be taken by Chinese citizens.
Asked what credentials she held, the White House passed along a statement from Zacharia, who received a bachelor of arts degree from Pepperdine University in 2007 and received her law degree from Pepperdine Caruso School of Law in 2011,  according to the school and her LinkedIn bio.
"I practiced international transaction law, with all the appropriate credentials," it read.
Steven Cheung, the White House communications director, added that Zacharia was "uniquely qualified and whip smart to help inform the American people about all the great things President Trump and his Administration have been doing, and she will do an incredible job as press secretary."
According to her LinkedIn profile, Zacharia has been the senior communications adviser at the Trump Media & Technology Group since June and spent two months as deputy assistant secretary for public affairs at the U.S. Department of Homeland Security earlier this year.
U.S. President Donald Trump is seen speaking with reporters on the South Lawn of the White House on Tuesday, with Zacharia looking on from nearby. (Manuel Balce Ceneta/The Associated Press)
From 2011 to 2013, it says, she served as an associate on the international practice team at the Zhong Lun Law Firm in Beijing. She also worked as the manager of fundraising and communications for Compassion for Migrant Children, which assists the children of migrant workers, from 2012 to 2013.
More recently, it says she served as general counsel for Fix California, a group started by Trump administration official Richard Grenell.
Neither the firm nor the two groups responded to questions about her tenure and background.
On Instagram, Zacharia describes herself as the White House press secretary, "Wife, Mom, & Lawyer" (with four heart emojis after "Mom").
And her official author page at the California Globe, where she wrote occasional commentary, says that, in addition to being a "regular commentator on Fox News, Newsmax," she has "extensive experience in political advocacy, international corporate law, and non-profit work, including time as outside counsel for the World Bank and IFC in Beijing."
Zacharia fails to impress in brief debut as White House press secretary
White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt to leave job at month's end, Trump says
A June 2026 press release from NovaRed Mining Inc. announcing her appointment to the company's advisory board, which was first reported by Popular Information, said her "professional experience includes work related to international legal and financial transactions, including matters involving organizations associated with the World Bank Group and the International Finance Corporation during her tenure with Zhong Lun Law Firm in Beijing."
In announcing her hire on his social media site, Trump described Zacharia as "a distinguished Graduate of Pepperdine University, and the Pepperdine Caruso School of Law, an attorney, and a frequent Commentator on outlets, including Fox News and Newsmax."
"She has an unblemished record of support, and has been a loyal and brilliant supporter, right from the beginning. She is, likewise, a devoted fan and member of MAGA!" he added.
Zacharia is not listed as a member of the state bar in California, where she currently resides, according to a public database.
Rick Coca, a spokesperson for the State Bar of California, the regulatory agency that oversees state licensing, said in a statement that it has "no record of Kate Sharon Zacharia or Kate Sharon Black" or any version of her married or maiden names "having been licensed to practice law in California."
Popular Information said the same was the case in all 50 states it had queried, plus Washington, D.C.
In response, the watchdog group Campaign for Accountability (CfA) filed a complaint Wednesday with the State Bar of California asking it to investigate whether Zacharia misrepresented herself as a lawyer in violation of California law.
"In California, calling yourself a lawyer without a license isn't puffery; it's a crime. The State Bar should investigate whether Ms. Zacharia has misled the public about her credentials and hold her accountable if she has," said CfA executive director Michelle Kuppersmith in a statement.
The State Bar said it could not confirm whether it had received the complaint or were conducting an investigation, citing confidentiality laws.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic Says Revenue Jumped 45% to $16.8 Billion in Third Quarter
articles.title_zh: Anthropic Says Revenue Jumped 45% to $16.8 Billion in Third Quarter
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Anthropic's (ANTH.PVT) Q3 revenue climbed to $16.8 billion, up from $11.5 billion in the second quarter.
The AI startup revealed the news to investors during a closed meeting, noting that it is also profitable on an adjusted basis, according to The Financial Times .
The news comes as Wall Street awaits Anthropic's public S-1 filing. The company p rivately filed the paperwork with the Securities and Exchange Commission on June 1.
Anthropic is projected to kick off its highly anticipated initial public offering (IPO) sometime this fall, with the Street eyeing a record $2 trillion valuation.
The latest revenue numbers come after the Financial Tim es reported that investors revised their estimates for Anthropic rival OpenAI's annualized revenue downward from $70 billion to $50 billion .
Investors, the report says, initially miscalculated OpenAI's numbers while attempting to match them to Anthropic's revenue run rate, resulting in a massive $20 billion swing.
While Anthropic is ramping up for its IPO, OpenAI is holding off on its until early 2027. According to Bloomberg , the company is instead looking to raise $30 billion at a $1.4 trillion valuation.
The two AI companies, as well as Meta ( META ) and Google ( GOOG ), have faced mounting pressure in recent months after reporting that their respective AI models broke free of containment and hacked into third-party websites and networks.
That's led to increased calls for regulations around AI models and their use. But President Trump has pushed back, opting for self-regulation among the companies.
Earlier this month, Trump convened a meeting of leading AI executives, including Amodei, at which they signed what Trump called a "morally binding" agreement to have independent auditors review their models for suspicious behavior.
Anthropic and OpenAI are also contending with a growing pricing war among AI model makers. With "tokenmaxxing" in the rearview, AI customers are looking for ways to save on AI expenses, whether that's through open-weight models from China or less expensive closed models from leading US labs.
Last week, Anthropic debuted its Claude Haiku 5.5 , saying it costs an average of 75% less than Haiku 4.5. Customers pay $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per output token. That's in line with rival OpenAI's ( OPAI.PVT ) smallest model, GPT-6 Luna.
Tokens are a measure of AI usage and represent portions of or entire words users type into prompt boxes and the responses the AI spits back out.
This story has been updated to reflect Wall Street's projected IPO valuation for Anthropic .

articles.title_orig: Could the Taliban’s new road to China drive negotiating power?
articles.title_zh: Could the Taliban’s new road to China drive negotiating power?
articles.content_orig:
Badakhshan Province, 4 October 2026, covering the Wakhan Corridor and Pamir region in Afghanistan (Javid Ashna via Getty Images)
In treacherous terrain, the Taliban has carved a path to potentially strengthen its position with China and against Pakistan.
Subscribe to The Informer for monthly expert analysis, and to Events for advance notice of visiting world leaders and distinguished guests.
You may unsubscribe from Lowy Institute newsletters at any time. For information on our privacy practices and how to unsubscribe, see our Privacy Policy .
Could the Taliban’s new road to China drive negotiating power?
The Taliban regime in Afghanistan has spent 365 million Afghanis – about US$5.5 million – building a road through one of the most remote corners of the country towards the Chinese border. It may turn out to be little more than a rough mountain road. But it could also give Afghanistan something it lacks: leverage.
At the northeastern edge of Afghanistan in the Wakhan Corridor, (Opens in new window) this new road is quietly changing the strategic geography. The Taliban's Ministry of Rural Rehabilitation and Development inaugurated (Opens in new window) the 121-kilometre gravel road on 4 October 2026, running from Broghil in Wakhan district to China’s border. The route includes four bridges, 66 culverts and more than 3,000 metres of retaining walls.
The road does not yet mean that Afghan trucks can simply drive into China, and there is no commercial border crossing. But it brings Afghanistan physically closer to a country that has become increasingly important to the Taliban's regional diplomacy. That possibility matters.
For years, Afghanistan has depended heavily on Pakistan for access to international markets. That dependence has become uncomfortable as relations between Kabul and Islamabad have deteriorated. The two countries shut major border crossings after deadly fighting in October 2025, disrupting bilateral trade and leaving hundreds of trucks stranded. The closure exposed how vulnerable Afghanistan remains to decisions made by its neighbour.
The consequences have gone beyond trade and impacts citizens. Before the closure, more than 70% (Opens in new window) of medicines used in Afghanistan were imported from Pakistan, according to the European Union Agency for Asylum. So, the attraction of another route is obvious.
The Wakhan Corridor is a narrow strip of Afghan territory extending eastwards between Tajikistan and Pakistan before reaching China's Xinjiang region. Its strategic importance is hardly new (Opens in new window) . During the 19th century’s Great Game era, it served as a buffer between the British Empire in India and the Russian Empire to the north.
The mountains that once made Wakhan useful as a buffer also made it extraordinarily difficult to reach. High passes, severe winters and poor infrastructure have kept the corridor isolated. The new road does not change that geography, but it does begin to work around it, and Beijing has been paying attention.
In February, Afghanistan's ambassador to China, Mawlawi Asadullah Bilal Karimi, met Liu Jinsong, head of the Department of Asian Affairs at China's foreign ministry. According to Chinese and Afghan accounts, the discussions included China-Afghanistan relations. Afghan reporting also said activation of the Wakhan Corridor was discussed.
In March, Afghanistan’s Acting Minister of Commerce Nooruddin Azizi also met China's Special Representative in Kabul, Yu Xiaoyong (Opens in new window) in Kabul to discuss connectivity and transit.
While this demonstrates diplomacy around the idea, there is a distinction between a road reaching China, and China agreeing to open a full commercial crossing. Beijing has made no public commitment to do so, and that is likely to remain the challenge.
A functioning trade route would require customs facilities, security arrangements and infrastructure, as well as a road capable of handling sustained commercial traffic. A high-altitude gravel road through the Pamirs is a different proposition from a modern trade corridor.
China's calculations are likely to be cautious for another reason: security. (Opens in new window) Beijing has maintained pragmatic relations with the Taliban while stressing its concerns about militant groups operating from Afghan territory, particularly those that could threaten China's Xinjiang region. China has also supported security cooperation along the Wakhan frontier. In 2025, China’s Foreign Minister Wang Yi (Opens in new window) said Beijing supported the resumption of bilateral patrols in the corridor and called for stronger Afghan action against the East Turkestan Islamic Movement and other militant groups.
For Beijing, therefore, the road is not simply about moving goods. It is also about what happens in the mountains beside Xinjiang. This is where the road becomes more interesting than its modest size suggests.
The new road does not change that geography, but it does begin to work around it, and Beijing has been paying attention.
Afghanistan has long been described as a potential bridge between Central Asia, China, South Asia and the Middle East. Its geography offers that possibility, but decades of war, political instability and inadequate infrastructure have prevented it from becoming reality. The Taliban now appears determined to test that proposition. (Opens in new window)
The most ambitious possibility would be a wider network linking China through Afghanistan to Iran and the Arabian Sea. Afghanistan already has access to Iran's Chabahar port, which offers an alternative to Pakistan's seaports. But that route has also been subject to geopolitical uncertainty, making the search for multiple routes more significant. But it would be a mistake to portray the Wakhan road as a ready-made alternative to Pakistan's ports, as the road is only the first piece of a larger puzzle.
Beijing may see value in greater economic access to Afghanistan. It may also see strategic value in having another potential connection to Central Asia and the wider region. But China has shown little appetite for taking unnecessary risks in Afghanistan. The road therefore matters less because it guarantees trade than because it creates possibility.
For Kabul, the symbolism is powerful. The Taliban can point to a domestically funded infrastructure project reaching towards China at a time when Afghanistan remains internationally isolated. More practically, it gives Kabul a card to play in its difficult relationship with Pakistan.
Shadi Khan Saif is a Melbourne-based journalist and a former Afghanistan/Pakistan correspondent for Reuters and Deutsche Welle.

articles.title_orig: Nasdaq ends sharply lower as hot inflation data stirs rate-hike worries
articles.title_zh: Nasdaq ends sharply lower as hot inflation data stirs rate-hike worries
articles.content_orig:
U.S. consumers are in the midst of one of the longest stretches of elevated inflation of the past century. Some are beginning to act like it's a new normal, raising alarm bells for members of the Federal Reserve .
Wednesday's consumer price index release showed a 3.7% increase year over year in September. CPI has now registered around 65 months — that's more than five years — of consecutive annual readings above 2%, a widely accepted target for inflation in the U.S.
This yearslong spell of high inflation has cast a dark cloud over everyday Americans' view of the economy, and could shape everything from how they budget to how they vote in next month's midterm elections. At the Fed, leaders are left questioning whether consumers' inflationary expectations are becoming too entrenched to rein in.
"They're starting to accept high inflation as just a fact of life," Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack wrote in a social media post last week. "That's concerning."
The current streak of stubborn inflation ranks among the most persistent in modern U.S. history.
The uninterrupted string of above-2% monthly CPI readings is the longest of the 21st century, according to a CNBC analysis of data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. The U.S. has seen longer periods on only two other occasions going back to the late 1940s.
Since inflation started running above 2% in early 2021, the average CPI reading has sat around 4.5%. The last time a streak had a mean reading that high was during a period ending in the 1980s .
Consumers are expecting inflation to accelerate. The one-year inflation outlook in September rose three-tenths of a percentage point to 3.9%, its highest reading in more than three years, according to the New York Fed's Survey of Consumer Expectations released last week.
One of the main worries of central bankers is that businesses and consumers may start permanently adjusting their behaviors to account for high prices. That can have ripple effects through the economy.
Businesses anticipating rising costs can preemptively hike prices for consumers. Workers expecting sticky inflation will ask for steeper pay raises to get ahead of any sticker shock.
All of this can make inflation a self-fulfilling prophecy, rendering the monetary policy tools at the Fed's disposal less effective in slowing price growth.
"Inflation expectations have to be anchored for monetary policy to affect the economy in an effective and predictable manner," said Gary Richardson, an economist and former historian at the Fed. "That's got to be number-one goal of any central bank."
At this juncture, Fed officials are closely watching to see if and how consumers respond to inflationary pressures.
During an event last month, Minneapolis Fed President Neel Kashkari said he heard from a labor union leader that inflation was "worse" than a recession for their members. Kashkari said that conversation influenced how he views the trade-off within the Fed's so-called dual mandate, which calls for stability in prices and maximum employment.
At a gathering of economists in Ohio this week, Hammack told the audience that she did not take the fact that long-run inflation expectations have stayed anchored "for granted." With each month that inflation comes in high, she warned that the risk grows of an "inflationary mindset" getting entrenched.
Economists widely view interest rate hikes as the Fed's main mechanism for slowing demand and, in turn, putting downward pressure on the annual pace of price growth. After hiking interest rates in September , Fed funds futures traders anticipate the central bank will raise borrowing costs further in December and in 2027.
In the long run, Diane Swonk, chief economist at consultancy KPMG, said interest rate hikes can benefit consumers by getting inflation under control. But in the near term, Swonk said consumers can feel more pressure due to higher borrowing costs.
"Inflation is like a cancer, and if you let it metastasize and go further, it's even worse," Swonk said. "Even when the cure hurts, it's better than letting it metastasize."
In Hammack's district, the Cleveland Fed chief said via social media that she's found evidence that residents are "choosing" rather than "trading down." For instance, she said they need to pick whether to pay for groceries or essential bills.
Consumers have lamented the cumulative price increases they now see in everyday life after the years-long run of high inflation. Adding to their woes is the fact that year-over-year inflation has run at a faster clip than wage growth in recent months, meaning the average consumer has lost purchasing power.
The University of Michigan's closely followed consumer sentiment survey earlier this year fell to the lowest levels ever seen . The highest share of respondents citing high prices as a reason for having worse personal finances surpassed 50% for the first time on record in 2026.
High prices are "dominating consumer thinking," said Joanne Hsu, the director of Michigan's survey. "They still consider it an unacceptable fact of life."
Compared with Democrats, consumer sentiment has tumbled more sharply among Republicans and independents this year. The question now is if voters angered about the rising cost of living will shift control in Washington away from Republicans and President Donald Trump in the midterm election.
Despite those glum outlooks, economists say that everyday Americans shouldn't bank on prices coming down from current levels. Deflation — which is when annual price growth falls below 0% — could put the national economy on a downward spiral.
Instead, their hope should be that inflation's 12-month growth rate can cool to levels below the pace of pay increases. If that happens for a long enough period, the higher wages and increased purchasing power would leave shoppers better equipped for today's prices.
Olena Nicks, an analyst and local lawmaker in Long Island, New York, is one of those consumers tightening the purse strings in the face of lofty prices. Nicks said she's specifically noticed steep price increases over recent years in the grocery store produce aisle and when looking at airline flights for vacations.
In response, the 34-year-old said she's cut back on purchasing meals at restaurants or from fast-food chains. Her friend group has forgone leisure activities like bowling, opting instead for less-costly nights spent in someone's home.
"Frustrated is an understatement," Nicks said. "It feels like you're stuck."

articles.title_orig: Sexual assault reported at frat house near University of Chicago
articles.title_zh: Sexual assault reported at frat house near University of Chicago
articles.content_orig:
Alleged assault follows report of gang-rape at frat house at Cornell, which ignited national uproar and criticism online
A 21-year-old woman reported being sexually assaulted last weekend at a fraternity house near the University of Chicago , as Greek life nationwide faces renewed scrutiny for recurrent misconduct.
The incident allegedly took place on Sunday at about 1.50am at the off-campus Alpha Epsilon Pi residence, according to a university daily crime log.
In a police report obtained by the Chicago Sun-Times, the woman said she was “not fully conscious” when she was found partially undressed inside a bathroom with a man, who was also semi-nude.
She told police, according to the report, that a group had blocked her friends, at first, from entering the bathroom.
A person of interest has been identified, according to university officials.
The individual is not a student and has been banned from campus, they announced on Wednesday.
No one is in custody, Chicago police said on Wednesday afternoon, adding that an investigation remains ongoing.
Jonathan Pierce, a spokesperson for the fraternity, said on Wednesday there was no evidence its members had participated in the assault or were aware of it.
“When AEPi members (there were several “sober monitors” during the party, including the chapter’s safety officer) became aware of the victim’s report, they offered assistance by providing food and water and even loaned a shirt to the victim as she reported being cold while she waited outside for emergency response,” Pierce said.
“We are pleased that the alleged assailant has been identified and hope that the victim can find some solace in knowing that justice is being done.”
The alleged assault follows a harrowing report of a gang-rape at a Cornell University fraternity house in 2024. Recent news of the purported attack ignited national uproar and criticism of the Ivy League school’s perceived leniency toward the alleged offenders.
New York state prosecutors have reopened an investigation into the report.
Under mounting backlash, Cornell has also suspended all fraternity parties for the remainder of the academic year, as it assesses the safety of its Greek societies.
Last week, the University of Arizona took a similar move, halting all fraternity activity in the wake of several hazing and physical assault allegations, including accusations of a Greek organization coercing recruits into binge drinking and swallowing live goldfish.

articles.title_orig: SC US Senate campaign escalates on China, law enforcement
articles.title_zh: SC US Senate campaign escalates on China, law enforcement
articles.content_orig:
On Wednesday, the war of words ramped up across the Palmetto State between U.S. Senate candidates, Republican Sen. Darline Graham and her Democratic challenger, Dr. Annie Andrews.
The candidates held dueling events in the Lowcountry and Upstate, as they look to get any edge with undecided voters in a race recent polls show is a close contest.
The increasingly heated campaign rhetoric and back-and-forth tied to China, foreign policy, and law enforcement comes less than a week before the start of early voting and less than three weeks until Election Day.
“National security isn’t an elective in this job," Andrews said during an event Wednesday morning in Charleston. There, she cited a recent Washington Post report that claimed Graham's husband is an executive at a company connected to Chinese weapons manufacturing.
Andrews said that the senator's family should cut any business ties to China and that Graham should recuse herself from any votes involving trade with China or Chinese military policy.
“I think it’s just important that we always put America first, American interests first, American security interests, privacy interests, data security interests, first and foremost," Andrews said. "To me, it’s a non-story; I mean, she’s desperate obviously," Graham said, who responded to Andrews' claims at an event Wednesday afternoon in Spartanburg — and pushed back on the claims in the Washington Post article.
"Bringing my husband into this is absolutely wrong; he’s an employee at a company," Graham said. "He doesn’t own it, he doesn’t have any shares in the company, he’s never been to China, he doesn’t make decisions like that, so I think it’s completely unfair to my husband.” On Wednesday afternoon in Greenville, several sheriffs of Upstate counties also officially endorsed Graham, citing her commitment to law enforcement funding.
“We understand her support for law enforcement," Greenville County Sheriff Hobart Lewis said.
In response, an Andrews campaign spokesperson said Graham failed to sign on to legislation that would help police officers buy homes and strengthen collective bargaining protections.

articles.title_orig: Did Katie Zacharia pass the bar exam? What we know about her legal credentials
articles.title_zh: Did Katie Zacharia pass the bar exam? What we know about her legal credentials
articles.content_orig:
In October, social media posts questioned new White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia's claim that she passed the bar examination in China.
The posts emerged after several reports asked whether Zacharia had the credentials to practice law anywhere in the U.S., though she has repeatedly identified herself as a lawyer in the past, including in an archived version of her X profile and during a television interview .
When asked Oct. 13 where she passed the bar (the examination that allows people to practice law), Zacharia responded , "When I moved to China." She did not say she passed the bar in any U.S. state.
People on Facebook and Reddit expressed doubts, while Rep. Ted Lieu, a Democrat from California, wrote on X, " Are Katie Zacharia and trump lying when they say she is an attorney? " ( archived ):
Meanwhile, Snopes readers emailed and searched the website, asking us to examine whether Zacharia could have possibly passed the bar in China.
An extensive search turned up no evidence Zacharia was a member of any state bar in the U.S., nor in Washington, D.C. In addition, current Chinese law made it unlikely that she was ever in a position to pass China's examination to practice law, as she is not a Chinese national. There was no evidence that she could do when she lived there between 2011 and 2013, though China only formalized rules about foreign lawyers in 2017.
For this reason, we have left the claim unrated.
"I practiced international transaction law, with all the appropriate credentials," Katie Zacharia told Snopes in an emailed statement. Neither she nor the White House press office answered follow-up questions, nor did they share any documentation showing she could practice law as an attorney in good standing in any jurisdiction.
" Katie graduated with a JD [Juris Doctor, a law degree] from Caruso School of Law in 2011, and with a bachelor of arts in political science from Seaver College in 2007," a spokesperson for Pepperdine University wrote in an email to Snopes.
A sked whether Zacharia could have taken and passed China's law examination before 2017, John Ohnesorge , a law professor at the University of Wisconsin-Madison who researched Chinese regulations of lawyers, said in an email to Snopes, "There's no possibility that she passed the Chinese bar exam, ever."
"W hat she did in China was to work in an elite Chinese law firm on international business matters, and doing that kind of work does not really require being a member of a bar anywhere," he added.
We also searched lawyer directories across the U.S. and found no record of Katie Zacharia — also searching by her maiden name, Black — in any of them.
Zacharia's LinkedIn profile indicates she worked in China between 2011 and 2013, at Zhong Lun Law Firm .
In 2020, the Chinese Justice Observer — a consulting platform and analysis outlet about the Chinese legal system — said foreigners cannot practice law in China . In 2019, China established a pilot program to allow foreign lawyers to act as legal consultants in China, not lawyers, though one condition is that the person should have practiced as a lawyer in their home country for at least two years.
Even under this program, Zacharia could not have practiced as a legal consultant as she had not practiced law in the U.S. long enough after she graduated.
Zacharia's LinkedIn indicates she later worked as "general counsel" for Fix California , a conservative organization that aims at ensuring "election integrity." It is unclear how she could hold this position without having passed the state's bar examination. We reached out to Fix California asking for more details.
A sheet of advice for French lawyers seeking to work in China from 2017 confirms that only Chinese nationals can practice law in China. In other words, any foreign lawyer practicing in China can do so only with credentials from the countries where they obtained their degrees.
However, China's current rules were implemented in 2017 . Ohnesorge, who wrote a research paper in 2023 about the history of the regulation of lawyers in China, said this measure was most likely protectionistic.
"It's true that the 2017 regulation started requiring two years of practice in a home jurisdiction in order to qualify as a foreign legal consultant, but that's best understood as a protectionist measure used to keep Chinese firms from hiring too many foreign lawyers, not a requirement that actually makes any sense," Ohnesorge said via email. "People doing the work she did aren't really practicing the law of their home jurisdiction anyway, so why require that at all?"
For further reading, Snopes covered several rumors about Zacharia's predecessor, Karoline Leavitt , including the claim that she said the war in Iran would be over if President Donald Trump had "better intelligence."

articles.title_orig: Ilhan Omar’s phone seized and relatives subpoenaed in criminal inquiry, source says
articles.title_zh: Ilhan Omar’s phone seized and relatives subpoenaed in criminal inquiry, source says
articles.content_orig:
Federal authorities issued more than a dozen grand jury subpoenas in inquiry into potential immigration fraud
US politics live – latest updates
Federal authorities investigating the Minnesota representative Ilhan Omar seized the Democratic lawmaker’s phone and have issued more than a dozen grand jury subpoenas, including to some of her relatives, according to a person briefed on the inquiry.
The subpoenas were issued for a grand jury collecting evidence in Minnesota as federal authorities investigate potential fraud in Omar’s immigration paperwork, said the person, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss an ongoing investigation. The investigation led to federal agents searching Omar’s Washington DC home on Monday just weeks before the November midterms , in which Omar is seeking re-election.
The scope of the investigation into Omar is unclear, though the secretary of the Department of Homeland Security, Markwayne Mullin, has suggested that authorities were examining potential crimes related to her family’s immigration paperwork.
On Tuesday, Jeanine Pirro, the US attorney for the District of Columbia, said in a Fox News interview that “there are several investigations going on” related to Omar and that her office is also looking into issues concerning the lawmaker’s financial disclosures.
“If there was a crime that was committed, it will be prosecuted,” Pirro said.
The search of Omar’s home so close to next month’s midterm contests, which will determine control of the House and the Senate, was swiftly condemned by Democrats, who accused the administration of targeting the representative for political purposes. Omar, in a statement on X, called the search an “attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement”.
“For 10 years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation,” she said. “I will not be silenced.”
A phone message seeking comment was left on Wednesday with a representative for Omar.
after newsletter promotion
Though the Republican focus on Omar’s background dates back years, the search notably took place three weeks before the November midterms, in which Omar is seeking re-election. The justice department has historically sought to avoid public investigative actions involving a candidate within 60 days of a primary or general election.
Omar, who was first elected to the House in 2018, represents Minnesota’s fifth district, including Minneapolis. She is part of “the Squad” of progressive lawmakers who are a vibrant political force on the left wing of Congress but have also endured repeated attacks from Trump, dating back to his first term. She was one of the first two Muslim American women in the House and the first African refugee to be elected to Congress.

articles.title_orig: Mary Cassatt exhibit at Art Institute aims to recreate lost mural from 1893 World's Fair
articles.title_zh: Mary Cassatt exhibit at Art Institute aims to recreate lost mural from 1893 World's Fair
articles.content_orig:
The 1893 World's Fair looms large in Chicago history.
Now, one of its groundbreaking works of art is a centerpiece of a new exhibit at the Art Institute of Chicago — but there is one big problem.
At the heart of this exhibit at the Art Institute is a work that no longer exists.
"It's a tough problem for a curator to have, to center this story about a monumental mural without the mural," said Annelise Madsen with the Art Institute.
That mural, " Modern Woman " by Mary Cassatt, was from the 1893 World's Fair.
"It was Cassatt really scaling up her subject matter, what she had built her career portraying, the lives of everyday women, but giving that a sense of import, a sense of grandeur," Madsen said.
Cassatt now has her own exhibit at the Art Institute, which aims to recreate the form and spirit of the long-lost mural.
"What we do have are a lot of enticing traces," Madsen said. "We have archival material. We have reproductions of the mural that are in fair publications from the 1890s. We have letters by Cassatt."
The exhibit covers a lifetime of Cassatt's work beyond the missing mural — like the iconic painting, "The Child's Bath," from 1893.
"She was a fierce, independent woman and an artist of the time," Madsen said. "I think she was, first of all, showing us the impact of human connection."
Her impact still felt, even through a mural that we can't see.
"It's a Chicago story, and we, for that reason alone, we must embrace it. It's part of the history of this city."
Mary Cassatt actually helped the art institute get one of its signature works — El Greco's " The Assumption of the Virgin ."
In 1905, Cassatt wrote to the institute's president when the painting became available, saying it belonged there.
Cassatt's exhibit runs through January 3, 2027.

articles.title_orig: Ancient shipwreck discovered off Turkey claimed to be world’s oldest
articles.title_zh: Ancient shipwreck discovered off Turkey claimed to be world’s oldest
articles.content_orig:
Artefacts from the ship were found just off the coast of Kekova Island
The world's oldest shipwreck has been discovered off the coast of Turkey, archaeologists say.
They have dated it to between 4,400 and 4,700 years old, which is the Early Bronze Age, and is around the same time that the Great Pyramid was being built.
The ship's wooden structure has not survived, but the ceramic storage pots it was carrying were lying on the sea floor and, remarkably, some still contain traces of what they held inside.
The archaeologists who found the ship say it was about 10m in length and was a trade vessel carrying cargo across the Mediterranean Sea.
"The shipwreck is a time capsule at the bottom of the sea," said Prof Hakan Ãniz, from Akdeniz University in Turkey, who led the Mediterranean Archaeology Association expedition.
The divers found three stone anchors, as ships carried spares on long voyages
The wreck is close to the shore of Kekova Island in Antalya, Turkey. The artefacts lie scattered across an underwater slope,  just 30m beneath the waves.
Three large stone anchors were found, as well as more than 30 ceramic storage pots, called amphorae.
The fact that none of the ship's wood remained meant techniques like radiocarbon dating - which measures a form of carbon in organic materials - could not be used to determine its age.
Instead, archaeologists analysed the shape of the amphorae. Because pottery styles have changed over time, different styles are linked to particular periods.
The Kekova ceramics are distinctive, with two handles, a ridge in the middle and a flat base.
Ãniz said this design matched other amphorae unearthed in Egypt and the Middle East that were known to be 4,400-4,700 years old.
"Comparing the decoration techniquesâ¦ we can definitely say our wreck is Early Bronze Age. This is 100%."
The amphorae were recovered and taken on board the research ship
After thousands of years underwater, the fragile artefacts are now being carefully conserved
Divers from the expedition brought the pots up to the surface, where they are now being carefully conserved after so many thousands of years underwater.
Dr Karin Sowada, an archaeologist from Macquarie University, Australia, examined the amphorae after they were recovered. Some were intact and she was surprised to see they still contained a viscous, glossy residue.
"I looked inside and nearly fainted. I could not believe how much [residue] was visible. It wasn't just like spotsâ¦. a lot of this material was still remaining," she said.
The team is now working to find out exactly what was being carried in the amphorae.
"It could be olive oil, it could be wine, it could be tree resins," Sowada said.
"It's possible that [the residue] could actually be the result of reuse of the jars. I mean, these jars are huge - they're not things that you just ship away and then never see again. People would have emptied these jars on arrival and potentially used them for many, many, many years."
The wreck and its cargo are also shedding light on trade in the ancient world.
The archaeologists say the ship started its voyage from somewhere along the eastern coast of the Mediterranean.
They believe it was taking goods to either the ancient city of Troy, in what is now north-western Turkey, or to the Minoan people in Crete.
The divers worked underwater to carefully excavate the artefacts
Travelling by sea was fraught with danger, particularly around Kekova Island, where the strong currents and winds have claimed many ships.
There are hundreds of wrecks in the area, and the Mediterranean Archaeology Association specialises in finding and studying them.
Ãniz says that when he is diving on the wreck his first thoughts are about the lives of the people who were connected to this vessel.
"We are the first humans who [have] touched these objects after 5,000 years.
"We are always thinking of the sailors... the producers of the amphora and the person who carried the amphora on their shoulders to the ship, and the women who were waiting for their husbands, and they unfortunately couldn't go back."
The shipwreck is owned by the Turkish Ministry of Culture. Its minister Mehmet Nuri Ersoy said the artefacts that have been recovered would be put on display in the new Mediterranean Underwater Archaeology Museum in Antalya when it opens in the coming months.
The depth meant the divers could only spend 30 minutes at a time exploring it
The Kekova discovery now tops the list of the world's oldest shipwrecks.
Previously, the record holder was a wreck off the coast of Dokos, an island in southern Greece, which dates to about 4,200 years ago.
The oldest known intact shipwreck, where the wood is still preserved, was found in the Black Sea off the coast of Bulgaria. It dates to about 2,400 years ago.

Pentagon chief warns US risks falling behind China in drones, robotics and AI without major investment in military capabilities
US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has called a nearly US$1.5 trillion defence budget request “absolutely critical”, warning that whoever falls behind in autonomy, robotics and AI will fall “even further behind” as Washington eyes China’s rapid military modernisation.
Speaking at a panel discussion during the Association of the United States Army (AUSA) Annual Meeting and Exposition on Wednesday, Hegseth said that Project Agincourt, the Pentagon’s initiative to accelerate drone and autonomous warfare capabilities, is the “end state” of what the administration has focused on since “day one”.
Asked how significant the increase to nearly US$1.5 trillion in the defence budget is, Hegseth replied that it is “absolutely critical” and a “one-time generational investment” that gives Washington a chance to “fully rebuild” the military amid threats from adversaries.

articles.title_orig: Measles cases surge past 150 in Kentucky; big outbreak identified in one county
articles.title_zh: Measles cases surge past 150 in Kentucky; big outbreak identified in one county
articles.content_orig:
Just days after Kentucky's measles case count hit 100, dozens more have been reported.
As of Wednesday, the number of cases reported in the Commonwealth is now 157 for 2026.
Most of those come out of Laurel County, which had seven cases just a few days ago. Now, it has 56, according to the state's dashboard .
Laurel County is in southeast Kentucky,
The dashboard says that outbreak involves people who are unvaccinated from several large households that have been "isolated from the broader community."
In only one case did the person report having the full vaccine. One case had one MMR dose, and the rest didn't have any.
Of the total state count, nine of those cases have led to hospitalization.
So far, no deaths have been reported.
There were only 13 cases overall in 2025, and none were reported the year prior.
Measles is a disease caused by a highly contagious virus.
It is spread through the air when someone with measles sneezes, coughs, or breathes.
Symptoms include high fever, cough, runny nose, red and watery eyes, and rash. Tiny white spots can appear inside the mouth two to three days after symptoms begin.
The disease can be especially severe in infants, pregnant women, and people who have weakened immune systems.
While rare, measles can result in death.
Kentucky health officials have warned this is the highest case count in decades. Dr. Steve Stack, with the Kentucky Cabinet for Health and Family Services, along with other local health officials, has been encouraging people to get vaccinated.
"We do not need to have measles," Gov. Andy Beshear said last month. "We have a proven tool that for over a quarter century eliminated it from the United States. The only reason it's resurging now is because of, I think, negligent information and guidance being shared freely. We want people to not feel vilified or maligned. We want people to feel informed."

articles.title_orig: Mike Tomlin’s Minecraft World Is the Talk of the Internet, but How Good Is It Really?
articles.title_zh: Mike Tomlin’s Minecraft World Is the Talk of the Internet, but How Good Is It Really?
articles.content_orig:
Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.
Football coaches have the freedom to create their own worlds on the playing field. But retired Steelers legend Mike Tomlin took a different route — manifesting his vision block by block within a massive Minecraft city. What started as a shared family project with his children evolved into a solitary, 12-year labor of love. Now, the sheer depth of Tomlin’s digital city is capturing widespread attention online.
Tomlin served as the Steelers’ head coach for 19 seasons before resigning in January, having never finished with a losing record.
His video was released Oct. 1 and received more than 3 million views in less than two weeks. In the video, Tomlin shows off an expansive Minecraft city, complete with sports stadiums, high-rise apartments, homes and other buildings. He began working on the city about 12 years ago after watching his kids and their friends play Minecraft when they were in middle school, building it in the game’s creative mode with their help.
“I was mesmerized by what could occupy their attention for such large periods of time,” Tomlin says in the video. “I’m certainly not skilled enough in video game play or have the stick control to [play the game’s survival mode], so I got interested in this creative mode. I like to build, I’ve always had an interest in architecture, and so I started doing this creative city as a means to spend time with them.”
His kids eventually outgrew the game and moved on to different ones, high school and eventually college. That left Tomlin to work on the city by himself, which he did off and on for years while still coaching the Steelers.
“More than anything, it was therapeutic for me, some mindless entertainment,” Tomlin says. “I’m not a big TV watcher. It allowed me to detach from the realities and pressures of life.”
Tomlin spends the rest of the video showing viewers around the place, focusing on his basic, early-days architecture, penthouses, apartments and how he tried to design a solid urban space. He plans to release more videos to discuss different buildings, the city’s design and other elements of his sprawling city.
Leading up to the video’s release, there was no indication whatsoever that Mike Tomlin played computer games. That helped make his big Minecraft debut all the more delightful. The 54-year-old coach showed off thousands of hours of playtime in a 19-minute video, and no one could believe it.
“12 years of Minecraft? Didn’t you know this? Did nobody know this?” asked a shocked Ty Schmidt, producer and on-air personality of the Pat McAfee show, on an episode of the show.
The sports world finally saw what some Minecraft fans already knew: Tomlin’s dedication to the game is unmatched.
“We’re talking block by block,” McAfee said. “He had 14 30-story buildings around a body of water that he wanted to build his city around — one block at a time! They all got patios! He had a penthouse with a shark aquarium. It was unbelievable.”
Minecraft fans, too, showed up to explore the coach’s dazzling feat. Many were surprised to learn that he built this on the Bedrock edition of the game using a video game console, beginning with PlayStation 3 before moving on to PlayStation 4 and 5. That means Tomlin didn’t have access to the mods that many builders use in the Java version of the game on PC, or the freedom that a mouse and keyboard provide. He built his city one brick at a time on a PlayStation controller.
Tomlin was initially unaware of his viral fame. In an interview on Late Night with Seth Meyers, Tomlin said he was at a gala with his phone off when the video went live, and it wasn’t until later that his kids told him about the massive response. Tomlin had caught up by the time he appeared on Football Night in America with NBC on Sunday night.
“I’m appreciating all of this, to be quite honest with you,” Tomlin said during the broadcast.
The spectacle of Tomlin’s Minecraft city is one of those wholesome events that had viewers smiling all weekend, except a few Steelers fans who were probably already pretty mad about losing to the Cleveland Browns less than 24 hours after the video was released. That didn’t stop a lot of people from wondering whether Tomlin’s city is actually as good as it looks. It turns out that most of the Internet agrees that it lives up to the hype.
“From my understanding, [it’s a] phenomenal Minecraft city,” McAfee said. “Like, as I was watching it, I was like, man, the attention to detail [is outstanding].”
Noted Minecraft city builder Alpine1 was one of the first to create his own video on the topic, and he was impressed. He had some suggestions for Tomlin, recommending that the coach consider using glass panes instead of glass blocks and more sophisticated floor designs, such as installing tile floors in showers. But Alpine1 did note that Tomlin likely started building the city before many modern building tools were available to Minecraft players.
“This is really awesome to see,” Alpine1 said in the video. “I’ve been advocating for people to build Minecraft cities for years because there’s so much you can do… and I think Mike has really captured this.”
Zach Nagel, an architecture student from the University of Cincinnati’s School of Architecture and Interior Design, also took a stab at analyzing Tomlin’s city in a separate video . He noted that Tomlin used some concepts that are actually practiced in architecture, specifically adding a penthouse with an aquarium right across the street from a full-sized aquarium.
“Now, what Coach Tomlin is talking about here, having a central theme to the building, is a term that we use in architecture as well, the parti ,” Nagel says. “If you talk to 20 architects and ask them to give a definition of a parti, you might get 20 pretty different answers. At its [simplest], a parti is a single idea or scheme that drives all of the decisions you make in a building.”
Nagel goes on to praise Tomlin for not only considering the building’s exterior appearance but also its interior design and the functional needs of the city’s fictional residents. He says that a lot of Tomlin’s design choices and approach are in line with what some architects use.
“In another world, he could’ve totally gone down this career path had he wanted to,” Nagel says. “And I’m glad to see that Minecraft remains such an accessible tool for those who want to shape the environment around them.”

articles.title_orig: Capitol agenda: Some Republicans write off the House - Live Updates
articles.title_zh: Capitol agenda: Some Republicans write off the House - Live Updates
articles.content_orig:
Some Republicans in the House of Representatives have secretly admitted that they will lose the majority in the midterm elections this November, according to a new report.
President Donald Trump has been fiercely campaigning for GOP candidates in red states that would normally be easy for Republicans to win. Trump has recently held rallies in Texas, Ohio and Alaska to stump for Republican Senate candidates, but members of his party are reportedly worried that the House will slip through their fingers.
Five senior Republicans on Capitol Hill anonymously aired their concerns to Politico , with one saying that the party just hopes to "save as many Republican seats as we can."
"President Trump has made this election all about himself," the House Republican said. "Now we have to survive that political storm."
White House Assistant Press Secretary Liz Huston told The Independent , "President Trump is committed to maintaining Republican majorities in both the House and Senate."
Some Republicans in the House of Representatives have secretly admitted that they will lose the majority in the midterm elections this November, according to a new report (AFP via Getty Images)
Term-limited Trump has been traveling across the U.S. to plead with his supporters to vote Republican.
"I want you to do me one big favor — pretend that I'm on the ballot because here's what happens. Every time I've been on the ballot, we win," the president said at his rally in Wasilla, Alaska, on Tuesday.
But the president is struggling with record-low approval ratings amid an unpopular Iran war and a high cost of living.
Sixty-five percent of Americans disapproved of Trump's job as president, while just 32 percent approved in a recent Reuters /Ipsos poll.
Trump has even resorted to promising Americans $5,000 checks if Republicans keep control of Congress, which critics have called a bribe .
"If Republicans win the House of Representatives and the Senate, I'm going to give all adult citizens in the United States $5,000," the president said in Alaska.
Five senior Republicans on Capitol Hill reportedly aired their concerns, with one saying that the party just hopes to 'save as many Republican seats as we can' (AFP via Getty Images)
Despite Trump's best efforts, some congressional Republicans are convinced they won't be able to pull off a big enough win.
The Congressional Leadership Fund, the leading super PAC supporting House Republican candidates, canceled advertising in Nebraska and Iowa to put the money toward other races, Politico reported. The Senate Leadership Fund, the main super PAC backing GOP Senate candidates, then reportedly took the airtime to support Republicans running for Senate seats in those states.
"These are not the moves of a party that's going to keep the House," another Republican lawmaker told Politico.
The Congressional Leadership Fund told the outlet it was unwavering in its fight to keep control of the House.
The super PAC's president, Chris Winkelman, said the goal is to "keep the pressure on the most vulnerable Democrats and preserve a path to 218 seats."
Term-limited Trump has been traveling across the U.S. to plead with his supporters to vote Republican, telling them to 'pretend that I'm on the ballot' (AFP via Getty Images)
Trump was in Bullhead City, Arizona, Wednesday to campaign for Congressman Andy Biggs, who is running against Democratic incumbent Katie Hobbs for governor, and congressional candidates Mark Lamb and Abe Hamadeh.
At the rally, Trump called Hobbs "dumb" and contrasted her intelligence with that of his on-and-off friend , tech billionaire Elon Musk .
"I know smart people. I deal from Elon [Musk] down to Katie [Hobbs]," Trump said. "Elon's 80 percent super genius — and 20 percent he got a little problem, I always tell him. He's a great guy, though."
He told the crowd, "We gotta elect" Biggs. "I'm here to help him and some of your great congressmen," the president said.

articles.title_orig: Epic says its new vibe-coded Epic Games Launcher is faster than Steam
articles.title_zh: Epic says its new vibe-coded Epic Games Launcher is faster than Steam
articles.content_orig:
Nearly eight years after Epic took on Steam with its own Game Store and launcher, the Fortnite maker is deploying a new tool to give it an edge over Valve: vibe coding.
In announcing the new publicly available “Preview” build of its Epic Games Launcher, Epic writes that “programming is hard. So, instead of doing that, we vibe coded a new Epic Games Launcher that’s way faster and more responsive than the current one, and has a new look.” And while that might sound a little tongue-in-cheek, Epic Games Store General Manager and VP Martin Keely told PC Gamer that the team “started from scratch” and used AI as “a tool to write and review new features and new capabilities from the ground up in a different tech stack than what we had previously.” The goal, Keely said, was to “look at functionality that existed [in the current Epic Games Launcher] and [say] we want to replicate that, but not the code itself.”
Speaking to IGN , Keely clarified that using AI to code the new Launcher “made us more efficient and allowed a small team to rewrite the code base and be able to launch it faster across platforms, support Windows and Mac, and we’re going to have a Linux version as well.”
We vibe coded the Epic Games Launcher to be faster than the other guy.
Don’t believe us? Test it out for yourself in Preview: https://t.co/pdtAeEIri4 https://t.co/aMxojUUVPV
— Epic Games Store (@EpicGames) October 14, 2026
The focus on startup speed extends to Epic’s social media announcement , which once again stresses that “we vibe coded the Epic Games Launcher to be faster than the other guy.” Ars’s own testing confirms that the new Launcher goes from a cold start to the store page a few seconds faster than Steam (assuming no login or update issues get in the way). Epic also claims the new Launcher can restore from the system tray to the Library screen slightly faster than Steam, though the claimed difference of 0.06 seconds in this seems so small as to be unnoticeable (and was in our testing).
Epic announced a ground-up “storefront rearchitecture” and “Launcher V2 private Beta” in an Unreal Fest presentation in June . At the time, the company said the new Launcher would have “5x faster cold start” times and help solve challenges that “every developer in this room and every player” has experienced with the current Launcher.
The term “vibe coding” still carries heavy connotations of quickly thrown-together slop that could hide crucial errors beneath the surface. On social media, Epic warns that its Launcher Preview “will have some bugs” that early testers can help squash with a feedback form. The announcement post also warns that the vibe-coded Preview is currently “light on features”— an FAQ clarifies that “certain social features and account management options” haven’t made it over from the legacy version just yet.
That said, the new Preview launcher adds some long-requested features like a Recent Games list and a centralized downloads hub for tracking network activity. And Epic writes that it is “working toward feature parity” between the new Launcher and the old one.
Epic’s release of the new “vibe coded” Launcher preview comes just days after a Bloomberg report suggesting the company is pivoting to an “AI first” development model for an upcoming Star Wars and Marvel-themed shooter. “We have a huge pivot underway here at Epic, moving developers around to retool for maximum AI acceleration,” Epic CEO Tim Sweeney wrote on social media on Monday. “The aim isn’t to do the same stuff with fewer people, but to enable everyone here to build MORE and BETTER stuff, and to bring the benefits to all teams using Unreal.”
